past_paper_mcqs.stem_text: If a planet comes closer to the Sun, then the planet will
options: D. keep moving with the same speed.
past_paper_mcqs.explanation: According to Kepler's Second Law of Planetary Motion (Law of Areas) and conservation of angular momentum, as a planet gets closer to the Sun (perihelion), its orbital speed increases.

past_paper_mcqs.stem_text: The gravitational force between two objects is directly proportional to the
options: D. square of the distance between them.
past_paper_mcqs.explanation: According to Newton's Law of Gravitation, the gravitational force $F$ between two point masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ separated by a distance $r$ is given by $F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$. Thus, the force is directly proportional to the product of their masses.

past_paper_mcqs.stem_text: A car travels a distance of 150 m in the direction of a constant force of 50 N. The work done on the car is
past_paper_mcqs.explanation: Work done ($W$) is given by the formula $W = F \times d$. Here, Force $F = 50\text{ N}$ and distance $d = 150\text{ m}$. $W = 50\text{ N} \times 150\text{ m} = 7500\text{ J}$.

past_paper_mcqs.stem_text: A car has stopped after screeching to avoid a crash with a van. With reference to the given situation, the kinetic energy of the car will then be converted into
past_paper_mcqs.explanation: When a car screeches to a stop, friction between the tires and the road generates thermal energy (heat) and the screeching noise produces sound energy.

past_paper_mcqs.explanation: In physics, work is done whenever a force acting on a body displaces it in the direction of the force ($W = Fd$).

crqs.question: Describe renewable and non-renewable sources of energy and give FOUR examples of each.
crqs.answer: Renewable sources are naturally replenished on a human timescale (solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal). Non-renewable sources exist in finite reserves and deplete with use (coal, petroleum, natural gas, uranium nuclear fuel).
crqs.source: AKU-EB SSC-I Model Paper II Q.7(a)

erqs.question:
The diagram shows a block is dropped from a point A and moves to a point B.

i. Calculate the change in potential energy (P.E.) of the block at point B with respect to ground. (3 Marks)
ii. Calculate the velocity of the block when it reaches to the point B. (3 Marks)

(Note: Take the value of acceleration due to gravity '$g$' as $10\text{ m/s}^2$.)
erqs.question_text:
The diagram shows a block is dropped from a point A and moves to a point B.

i. Calculate the change in potential energy (P.E.) of the block at point B with respect to ground. (3 Marks)
ii. Calculate the velocity of the block when it reaches to the point B. (3 Marks)

(Note: Take the value of acceleration due to gravity '$g$' as $10\text{ m/s}^2$.)

rubric.description: 1 mark for extracting the correct data: m = 10 kg, g = 10 m/s², vertical drop h = 30 m - 10 m = 20 m.
1 mark for the correct potential energy formula: P.E. = mgh.
1 mark for the correct change in potential energy from A to B: ΔP.E. = 10 × 10 × 20 = 2000 J.
1 mark for equating loss in P.E. to gain in K.E. (K.E. = P.E.) or using 2gh = v_f² - v_i².
1 mark for writing K.E. = ½mv² (or substituting into 2gh = v_f²).
1 mark for the correct velocity at point B: v = √(2 × 10 × 20) = √400 = 20 m/s.

erqs.answer:
**Given Data:**
Mass of block ($m$) = $10\text{ kg}$
Height at point A ($h_A$) = $30\text{ m}$
Height at point B ($h_B$) = $10\text{ m}$
Vertical distance fallen from A to B ($h = h_A - h_B$) = $30\text{ m} - 10\text{ m} = 20\text{ m}$
Acceleration due to gravity ($g$) = $10\text{ m/s}^2$

**(i) Change in Potential Energy ($\Delta P.E.$) of the block from A to B:**
$\Delta P.E. = mgh = 10\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m/s}^2 \times (30 - 10)\text{ m} = 10 \times 10 \times 20 = 2000\text{ J}$
*(Note: The potential energy remaining at point B with respect to the ground is $P.E._B = mgh_B = 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000\text{ J}$, and the loss/change in P.E. from A to B is $3000\text{ J} - 1000\text{ J} = 2000\text{ J}$.)*

**(ii) Velocity of the block at point B ($v_f$):**
By conservation of energy ($\text{Gain in } K.E. = \text{Loss in } P.E.$) or the third equation of motion ($2gh = v_f^2 - v_i^2$ with $v_i = 0$):
$\frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 = 2000\text{ J} \implies v_f^2 = \frac{2 \times 2000}{10} = 400$
$v_f = \sqrt{400} = 20\text{ m/s}$.

numericals.problem:
The diagram shows a block is dropped from a point A and moves to a point B.

i. Calculate the change in potential energy (P.E.) of the block at point B with respect to ground. (3 Marks)
ii. Calculate the velocity of the block when it reaches to the point B. (3 Marks)

(Note: Take the value of acceleration due to gravity '$g$' as $10\text{ m/s}^2$.)
numericals.solution:
**Given Data:**
Mass of block ($m$) = $10\text{ kg}$
Height at point A ($h_A$) = $30\text{ m}$
Height at point B ($h_B$) = $10\text{ m}$
Vertical distance fallen from A to B ($h = h_A - h_B$) = $30\text{ m} - 10\text{ m} = 20\text{ m}$
Acceleration due to gravity ($g$) = $10\text{ m/s}^2$

**(i) Change in Potential Energy ($\Delta P.E.$) of the block from A to B:**
$\Delta P.E. = mgh = 10\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m/s}^2 \times (30 - 10)\text{ m} = 10 \times 10 \times 20 = 2000\text{ J}$
*(Note: The potential energy remaining at point B with respect to the ground is $P.E._B = mgh_B = 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000\text{ J}$, and the loss/change in P.E. from A to B is $3000\text{ J} - 1000\text{ J} = 2000\text{ J}$.)*

**(ii) Velocity of the block at point B ($v_f$):**
By conservation of energy ($\text{Gain in } K.E. = \text{Loss in } P.E.$) or the third equation of motion ($2gh = v_f^2 - v_i^2$ with $v_i = 0$):
$\frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 = 2000\text{ J} \implies v_f^2 = \frac{2 \times 2000}{10} = 400$
$v_f = \sqrt{400} = 20\text{ m/s}$.

numericals.problem: Sara has mass of 30 kg. While running in the playground, she accelerates from 2 m/s to 4 m/s in 5 s. Calculate the power consumed in the given situation.
numericals.solution:
Given data:
Mass ($m$) = 30 kg
Initial velocity ($v_i$) = 2 m/s
Final velocity ($v_f$) = 4 m/s
Time ($t$) = 5 s

Work done ($W$) = Change in kinetic energy ($\Delta KE$)
$W = \frac{1}{2} m v_f^2 - \frac{1}{2} m v_i^2$
$W = \frac{1}{2} (30) (4)^2 - \frac{1}{2} (30) (2)^2$
$W = 15(16) - 15(4)$
$W = 240 - 60 = 180$ J

Power ($P$) = $\frac{W}{t}$
$P = \frac{180 \text{ J}}{5 \text{ s}} = 36$ W

numericals.problem: If a loading truck has an output of 3600 J and its efficiency is 50%, then the input provided to the truck will be
numericals.solution: Efficiency = $(\text{Output Energy} / \text{Input Energy}) \times 100$. Rearranging for Input Energy: $\text{Input} = (\text{Output} / \text{Efficiency}) \times 100 = (3600 / 50) \times 100 = 7200\text{ J}$.

numericals.solution: Kinetic Energy ($KE$) = $\frac{1}{2} m v^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5\text{ kg} \times (500\text{ m/s})^2 = 0.25 \times 250000 = 62500\text{ J}$.
